utterances.text: Witness, did something happen to Ymer Alushani during the offensive on Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was killed in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What happened with his body?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not certain about the date, but after three days, we dragged his body from Lapusnik because it remained there for three days. Ymer's body and his weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We buried him in Klecke.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you have a conversation with Celiku about recovering Ymer Alushani's body?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My uncle and my -- Ymer's uncle and brother. I only accompanied them. They talked. They came and said that they were not allowed to take the body because it was dangerous to go there, that is for living people to go and take a dead person. It was really very dangerous and it was not allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you there when the uncle and brother of Ymer had a conversation with Celiku or did you just hear about it later?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honour may I just intervene at this stage. It's -- nobody has pointed it out yet, but there is in fact another extraordinarily leading question. Did you have a conversation with Celiku? Whether the answer is worth anything of course I appreciate is for Your Honours, but effectively that is a question which seriously does not arise in that context. If the question is, And what happened after that? We buried him in Klecke, the next question should have been: And did you have conversations about this with anyone and so on. It's just worthless doing it in way, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think the question is built upon the preceding answer which was to a question about a conversation with Celiku. And the answer was that it was my uncle and brother. And I think that's what led to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just correct it that isn't actually what happened. I still have it on the screen the questions were: What happened with the body? What happened after that? Nothing about a conversation. And then there's the leading question: Did you have a conversation with Celiku? We really don't wish to intervene on these occasions. It is clearly leading. It is clearly not a sensible way of approaching this evidence and we restrain ourselves from repeating it, it happens so often. And we say the answer is worthless and there should be no question of that kind unless the foundation has been laid and it hasn't been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mansfield, I was merely transferring it's source of the problem. It wasn't perhaps the question you identified but the preceding one which was really the difficulty and but whichever it was I'm not resisting your proposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just try to be draw his attention to the topic and just move through it quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Drawing your attention to that topic is not something that I think you can reasonably anticipate to be acceptable to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, that's fine. I can go about it the way that has been proposed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You go about it however you feel so long as you don't lead on such a fairly critical issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine. I had not identified this as being a particularly critical issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, did have you any conversations about Ymer Alushani's body?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how it was translated, but I said the uncle, the brother and myself went to Klecke to talk with Celiku. I didn't go inside. I stayed out in the corridor talking with someone. His uncle and brother talked with Celiku and they received the answer I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you give us again the answer that they received from -- what they told to you about the answer that they received from Celiku.

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer from Celiku was, No, you shouldn't go there. He said that if some one of my soldiers will go there he will be shot. That was his reply. And this was confirmed by his brother later and all Ymer's comrades, all his unit knew that, because his uncle confirmed it too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you said that after you left Lapusnik you went to Berisa and then Novoselle. After that where did you go?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Lladrovc village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what did you do there?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Someone in Novoselle -- there was a doctor there, and he administered me the first aid. I got other clothes in Lladrovc. In the afternoon we buried a soldier who been killed on the 25th in Lapusnik and that was it. We buried Ali Zogaj that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what happened the next day?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed there in Lladrovc, until the 28th in the morning I stayed there. When I recovered I left with a tractor up to a place, to Terpeze. From there I started to walk on foot, to Klecke. On the way, Qerqiz gave me a lift in his jeep, I said. It was a white jeep, an old white jeep.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Klecke?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three, four, or five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Nekovce village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did you do in Nekovce?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We got together there with some soldiers from Lapusnik into a unit, and we took up positions at the entrance to Nekovce village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How long did you stay there in Nekovce?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the 20th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said that you got together there with some soldiers from Lapusnik into a unit. Approximately how many soldiers?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Eight persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did that number remain the same until the 20th of September?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe one or two others joined us, but usually we didn't -- weren't more than seven, eight, maximum nine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And generally what did you do during that time from -- up until the 20th of September?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were waiting to see what had happened, in August there was attack against the village, Nekovce, Kishna Reka, Shale, Bajice, and that day we were engaged in fighting all day in Nekovce valley. Only that unit. There was another unit in Nekovce, but that day they didn't take part in the fighting. They withdrew with the population to the mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did the unit and the population that withdrew to the mountains, did they ever return to Nekovce while you were there?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After the fighting that day, which as I said were strong fighting, several people got killed from Nekovce village. After some Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. days, the Serb forces withdrew. And after several days the population came back to their homes, one after the other. And the unit returned with the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did -- during this time up until the 20th of September, did you have any contact at all with Celiku?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And can you describe the nature of that contact?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a dispute between the unit that had returned, that one from Nekovce, and our unit. We had asked them to take positions in Divjak village but they had refused. They asked us to go to Divjak. We told them that, It's you left this place on the day of the fighting so it's you who should go to Divjak. We had a meeting. In that meeting we couldn't make a decision as to what to do so we had an argument over this issue. Again, Celiku disarmed some of them. Nine persons actually from that unit, the Nekovce unit were disarmed, he wanted to disarm two or three others from our unit, whereas me he asked me to go to another place with another person, to go to Terpeze.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall when this was?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think on the 9th -- I went to Terpeze on the 19th or the 20th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, did you stay in the Llap zone until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not until the end, because in the end of April I passed to Karadak zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During the time that you were in the Llap zone, did you see any prisons there?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where did you see them?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two persons were stopped and they were detained in Potok. These I have seen. As for two or three others they were kept in Burice village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And were these people, do you know if they were Serbs or Albanians?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All of them were Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you have any information on why they were being detained?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The two persons who were in Potok, they had created a unit in Brastice village, a KLA unit and they were arrested there allegedly for forming that unit out of their own accord. One had been an inspector in the Serb police. He was Albanian. And the other was a citizen from Pristina. In Burice village, there were some thieves were arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember when you saw the persons detained in Potok?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 5th I arrived Potok. On the 6th I saw them. The 6th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did there come an occasion when you had a dispute with a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It could have been a misunderstanding because they were free, they were in an oda where other soldiers were as well. Maybe guarded them. We went out in front of the prison to take a walk with a person who had been an inspector. And after half an hour, while I wanted to go back, two jeeps came. They took the prisoner away. As they explained it to me, they suspected that I might have want to the kill this police inspector. They thought -- they suspected that someone from Drenica had sent me to kill this inspector. This was not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where did this happen that you are describing?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Potok. On 6th of October. And on the same night I returned to Burice in order not to be in the same place with the others. And as I said, these two arrested persons were given back their weapons, and they formed a unit in the Llap territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did there come an occasion when you struck a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened in Burice, not in Potok after several days. It happened in Burice village. As I said, there were some thieves who had plundered the civilian population. And they were very provocative about the beard. No one in the Llap zone had beard. It was forbidden, and this was the argument, so I hit one of the prisoners several times, two or three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did you do that with your fist or with something else?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was something inside that I tried to get, and I wanted to hit him with that on his body, but I know that I slapped him. I didn't hit him with the fist. The intention was not to harm him, but just to stop him with the provocations and he stopped provoking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, with the assistance of the usher, I want to show you Prosecution Exhibit 169. And I'm going to ask you to turn to the back pages, 7029 to 7031.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And on the English translation it's pages 23 to 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, do you see on these pages there's some entries starting with 10 May, 18 May, 1998, 21 May. Do you see those entries? They go up to an entry for 28 July. And then one that's just marked July.

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, I can see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know when those entries were written in the book?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were written much later. It was loose paper, found in my pockets and they were most probably written in August or in September, in Nekovce. But just not to lose it, I wrote it in small sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when you say they were written in Nekovce in August or in September, is that in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can I draw your attention to the entry for 22 June. And if you could just read that entry, please.

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall I read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Please, if you could. Just the entry for 22 June.

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Everything took a different direction in the KLA now. The life of every soldier was becoming more than enough. In Celiku's zone, with different sorts of patrols or paroles. Controls and other types of masquerade."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember what this entry refers to?

utterances.speaker: Witness L-64 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This refers to shortly to some arrests that were being made; to disarmament in particular, of the soldiers, of those soldiers who had been disarmed. To such things. You could see that in Lapusnik they didn't bother much. They -- the soldiers were treated like a spending material [as interpreted]. Everything was in the hands of those who were in the command and about the command and above. Even if you had a need for food to go to your family, you had to wait for Qerqiz or someone else to get a permission just to go back home to intervene in case there was someone sick, and similar things.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you would like start tonight you are free to do so, Mr. Mansfield. But given the hour, it may be more practical if it were the morning -- tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. If I may. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. As there are only five or six minutes to go, we will adjourn now and continue tomorrow afternoon at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Can I just raise something before Your Honours rise. Sorry to delay you. Your Honours, we did our best on the end of last week in the absence of Mr. Limaj to give counsel's best assurances regarding the remainder of this week and what we anticipate and still anticipate to be the position. Your Honour, I don't know precisely how long Mr. Mansfield is go be, but he tells me as he told you the best part of tomorrow, and probably tomorrow. The assurances we gave as I say, remain the case. But, Your Honour I simply rise to say this: That in such an important case about such an important witness I know the Tribunal would not my lay client to feel that his counsel was in any way being rushed through what inevitably will be an important cross-examination. I shall as always endeavour not to duplicate what has gone before me, but Your Honours can anticipate from a three-day examination-in0chief there is an enormous amount of material that touches against the case against my client from the mouth of this witness. I know the Tribunal will not want to impose any undue pressure or indeed any pressure in those circumstances. May I please have liberty to raise this matter again, perhaps during the course of tomorrow to see how we are progressing. Leaving open the glimmer of a thought in the Tribunal's mind that if people have not made other arrangements, Thursday is an option. Or perhaps it is no longer is, in the Tribunal's mind. You will see why I raise this matter now out of an abundance of caution and somewhat diffidently, because I don't go behind anything that any of us have Defence bar said to this Court last week. And I hope nothing I said in any sense contradicts it. But it seemed to me that it was worth raising it, given that we had a moment or two tonight to spare, as it were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Topolski, thank you for that. As you appreciate, on Thursday the concern of the Chamber was to be sure of allowing adequate time because we anticipated that there would seem to be importance with this witness and the cross-examination. As matters eventuated, it was not possible to use anything of Thursday or Friday because of the problem of health. So that time was not lost unnecessarily, and we are now looking at three days of hearing this week, which you hoped would be enough, but may not prove to be enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I still hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I can only say that I have made arrangements about other cases for Thursday. I may be able to undo those arrangement but I haven't yet consulted with my two fellow Judges, so I don't know whether there will be any possibility of any sitting on Thursday. I think probably not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, thank you for that. And I will attempt to cut my cross to the cloth to the suit that is available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you for that. We will adjourn now. We will continue tomorrow at 2.15. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
